sources.text: AI for Tuberculosis Research Machine Learning Enzymes Tell Me More PLVis repository About Our Humble Beginnings In September 2023, we opened our doors at UC San Diego as a mixed computational and experimental group. Our mission is to bring cutting-edge AI for tuberculosis research — from predicting essential protein interactions to designing protein-based inhibitors. At the same time, we pursue foundational problems in biochemistry, with a focus on protein language models and the enzyme-to-substrate mapping challenge. The Computational Lab Our lab uses powerful computers to apply machine learning tools to the protein-small molecule (e.g. enzyme-substrate) mapping problem. We have our own GPU workstations and access to supercomputers at the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC). The Wet Lab Our wet lab focuses on enzyme biochemistry, where among other things, we: Validate computational predictions of enzyme function Generate new data to train our machine learning models Perform enzyme activity assays We collaborate with world-class LC-MS experts at UCSD to precisely measure enzyme activities and metabolites. Our values We strive for excellence in all we do. Our main goal is to nurture scientists and humans; high-quality research and publications naturally follow from this focus. We encourage the use of resources like Materials for Nurturing Scientists from Uri Alon's group to support this mission. We value community engagement through outreach activities and embrace diversity in all its forms. To enhance our scientific productivity and empower our trainees, we actively integrate AI tools, including large language models, into our work. His research is supported by an HHMI Hanna Gray fellowship. He is co-founder of Clubes de Ciencia Mexico, a non-profit STEM outreach organization. In his free time, he likes playing with his two kids and learning about trees and insects. Email: ajinich@health.ucsd.edu Erika Garay Email: ecgaray@health.ucsd.edu Melina Shamshoum Melina is a newly appointed postdoctoral fellow from Israel. She recently earned her Ph.D. in Biochemistry from the Weizmann Institute of Science under the supervision of Dr. Filipe Natalio. Her research focused on gaining a deeper understanding of the enzymatic mechanisms involved in cotton cellulose biosynthesis. She utilized cotton ovules as biofactories, integrating chemically synthesized sugars with desired functionalities to produce novel fibers with tailored properties. Her doctoral studies were funded by the prestigious Ariane de Rothschild Fellowship for Women in Science. Melina also holds an M.Sc. from the Weizmann Institute, where she worked under the supervision of Prof. Ron Milo. Her master's research focused on identifying and characterizing highly efficient Rubisco enzymes by systematically analyzing their natural sequence diversity, with the goal of enhancing photosynthetic efficiency and carbon fixation. During her graduate studies, Melina also conducted a research project in the lab of Prof. Ed Bayer at the Weizmann Institute, where she explored the deconstruction of cellulosic substrates and the enhancement of cellulose degradation processes. Her contributions have significantly advanced the fields of biofuels and renewable energy. Now based in California, Melina enjoys exploring San Diego and its surroundings with her husband and three children, discovering new travel spots and experiences. Email: Mshamshoum@health.ucsd.edu Ricardo Almada Monter Ricardo is a PhD student in UCSD's Computational Track of the Chemistry Department. Ricardo grew up in Xochimilco, Mexico City, and earned a bachelor’s in chemistry from Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) specializing in Computational Chemistry. He later earned a master’s degree in Theoretical Chemistry from the University of Chicago. Ricardo works in leveraging the power of Large Language Models with computational chemistry theories to predict the biophysical properties of enzymes, as well as implementing approaches to create chatbots for scientific research. Outside of the Lab, Ricardo spends his time walking around the neighborhood and places of interest. Email: ralmadamonter@ucsd.edu Adriana Siordia Adriana is a first-year PhD student in biochemistry at the University of California, San Diego. Originally from San Diego, California, they completed their undergraduate studies at Southwestern Community College before transferring to UCSD for their BS in Biochemistry. Adriana's research focuses on using protein language model (PLM) to forecast interactions between sterols/steroids and proteins. Outside of research, Adriana spends their time surfing, playing soccer, and running, while also watching "RuPaul's Drag Race" and supporting San Diego's local drag scene. Email: adsiordia@ucsd.edu Sarah Marta Veskimägi Sarah is currently a first-year PhD student in Chemical Biology at UCSD. She grew up in snowy Estonia, and before moving to sunny San Diego, she graduated Summa Cum Laude from Bates College in Maine with a BS in Biochemistry. Sarah's PhD research will combine her interests in drug development and enzyme-substrate interactions with machine learning models to better our understanding and treatment of diseases. When not in the lab, you can find Sarah hanging out with her friends, working on her latest craft project, or exploring the local farmers' market, gathering fresh produce for her next cooking adventure! Email: svesmikagi@ucsd.edu Nathaniel Roethler Nathaniel is currently a PhD student student in Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics (entered Fall 2023). He grew up in Bettendorf, IA, a small, heartland town along the Mississippi River. Before moving to UCSD, Nathaniel graduated from Loras College in Dubuque, IA with a B.S. in Biochemistry. Nathaniel’s research will utilize Protein Language Models and Machine Learning to develop tools to understand and investigate antimicrobial resistance by chemical group addition. When not in lab, you can find Nathaniel patrolling the dark streets of Grad Housing at night, wearing a black suit and speaking in a raspy voice. They think I’m hiding in the shadows… watching… waiting to strike… but I am the shadows. Email: nroethler@ucsd.edu Sarah Johnson Sarah obtained her bachelor’s at the University of Vermont, where she studied glia in fruit flies. As a research tech at Duke University, she investigated mechanisms of synaptogenesis and behavior. She is now developing multi-targeting protein binders to combat antibiotic resistance. In her free time, Sarah enjoys improving her Spanish, Mandarin, and Japanese, playing piano, listening to progressive rock, and drawing. Email: saj027@ucsd.edu Amanda Spencer I completed my Bachelor’s degree in Chemistry at Boise State University in 2022 and am currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Chemistry at the University of California, San Diego. Beyond academia, I’m passionate about the arts, frequently engaging in creating art, enjoying music, and attending concerts. I also value spending time in nature, particularly at the beach where I can enjoy the wildlife and natural scenery Email: a2spencer@ucsd.edu Seda Kavlak Seda is a master’s student in Bioinformatics at the University of Potsdam and a visiting scholar at UCSD. Her work focuses on advancing the Protein Language Visualizer (PLVis), a tool that leverages protein language models to explore proteomes. She discovered her passion for machine learning and AI during a primatology research project in West Africa, which inspired her transition from studying primate behavior to bioinformatics. Outside of research and programming, she enjoys lifting heavy weights, trying new food spots, and spending time around horses. Email: SKAVLAK@health.ucsd.edu Maeve O'Connor Maeve is a 4th year biochemistry student graduating in June of 2025. She plans to work as a pharmacy technician and continue her research during her gap year before she plans to attend pharmacy school. Maeve is investigating the azoreductase enzyme family through computational and classical biochemical methods. In her free time, Maeve loves to read fantasy novels, play board games, and try nee restaurants with friends! He intends on pursuing an advanced degree related to Biology, either in medicine or research. In his free time, you might see him on a run, cooking, or in line at CAVA whenever he’s not cooking. Email: abnambiar@ucsd.edu Javier Amaral I am a fourth-year undergraduate biochemistry major, originally from South San Francisco. I intend to attend medical school and become a doctor. I like to surf, hike, BBQ, and be in the great outdoors. Email: jamaral@ucsd.edu Akshay Uppal Akshay Uppal is an undergraduate research assistant in the Jinich Lab at UCSD. Coming from India, he travelled across the globe to pursue a B.S. in Data Science with a keen interest in biochemistry and chemistry. In the lab, he works on visualizations using python tools to make viewing protein structures easier and also help predict enzyme-substrate interactions. Out of the lab he is an avid sports fan mainly enjoying soccer, tennis, volleyball but at heart he is mainly a basketball player and is a warriors fan. Kate grew up in Shenzhen, China, and has lived in Orange County, California, since high school. In the Jinich Lab, she is developing a structural classification model to detect steroid-protein binding interactions. Outside the lab, Kate enjoys music, playing video games, and taking walks with her cat, Mos. He has prior experience in data science, AI, and microbiome research. Outside of academics, Tristan enjoys playing basketball and soccer, spending time at the beach, and cheering for the Los Angeles Lakers, Real Madrid, and Chelsea FC. She's particularly interested in enzyme function, cell biology, and human anatomy, and hopes to learn more as part of Jinich Lab. In her free time, she likes to play soccer as part of UCSD's Women's team, read, and go to the beach. Email: c8wilson@ucsd.edu Jimmy Che I am an undergraduate biochemistry major. I am currently a third year, and I find Artificial intelligence to be intriguing and would love to work in a career that harnesses Artificial Intelligence to accelerate clinical trials. Outside of academics, I like to workout at the gym, consume political commentary, and socialize with my friends Email: jiche@ucsd.edu Leonardo Calderon Leonardo is an undergraduate volunteer from Instituto Tecnológico de Tijuana, where he is currently pursuing a B.S. in Computer Systems Engineering. Born and raised in Tijuana, Mexico, Leonardo is particularly interested in artificial intelligence and machine learning applications to biochemistry and computational biology. Outside of the lab, Leonardo is a passionate fan of comics and movies. Members of the Jinich lab are strongly encouraged to actively participate in outreach activities, such as the Clubes de Ciencia Mexico program. Clubes de Ciencias México Founded in 2014 in Guanajuato, Mexico, Clubes de Ciencia has since grown to 9 cities and 8 Ibero-American countries. The program aims to broaden access to high-quality science education for motivated students at the high school and university levels. Through international academic collaborations, the program fosters scientific curiosity and supports the development of future leaders in science, technology, and innovation. Courses are led by volunteer instructors who are active researchers in their fields Learn More Teaching at UCSD We teach Chem 169/269: Applied Machine Learning and AI for Biochemistry, a hands-on course focused on applying modern AI to real biological data. Students work in teams to analyze protein language model embeddings, predict enzyme function, and explore tools like AlphaFold, UMAP, and contrastive learning — all in the context of cutting-edge biochemical problems. Veskimägi, Maeve O’Connor, Adriana Siordia, Nathaniel Roethler, Adrian Jinich Read more about this amazing work in the publisher page here The advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies and the availability of biological “big data” has accelerated the discovery of new protein sequences, making it challenging to keep pace with their functional annotation. To address this annotation challenge, techniques such as Sequence Similarity Networks (SSNs) have been employed to visually group proteins for faster identification. In this paper, we introduce an alternative visual analysis tool. Our simple and modular Protein Language Visualizer (PLVis) pipeline combines pre-trained PLM embeddings, dimensionality reduction algorithms and clustering methods to enable rapid assessment of proteins based on their neighbors. The resulting interactive visualizations can be enriched with multiple layers of biological and structural annotations. We present a head-to-head comparison of PLVis with SSNs and find concordant clustering patterns, with PLVis offering the additional advantage of revealing relationships between proteins that would appear as isolated nodes in an SSN.
